notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: omnis is stressed early in the line: the whole of Troy, not just some, lets go of its grief. It makes the coming disaster more tragic, since everyone is caught off guard.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: longo and luctu are separated across the line, so the "long grief" frames the sentence. The stretched-out phrase reflects the ten long years of war.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Teucer was the first king in the Troad, which was called the Teucris, the land of Teucer after him.

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense makes the opening of the gates happen before the reader's eyes, capturing the Trojans' sudden relief.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: panduntur is the first word of the line, so the throwing open of the gates bursts out with sudden excitement. Ironically, the Trojans are opening themselves to danger.

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense captures the Trojans' delight as they wander freely, which makes the later disaster all the more painful.

notes.label: Synecdoche
notes.body: Strictly implies ‘Dorian’, but is here used for the Greeks in general

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: desertos and locos are separated by videre, so the emptiness of the camp seems to spread across the phrase. The reader sees the Trojans gazing at the abandoned site.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated l sounds are soft and flowing. They suggest the calm, empty shore and the Trojans' relaxed mood.

notes.label: Variatio
notes.body: Virgil uses two different words for "left empty". The variety stresses how completely the Greeks seem to have gone.

notes.label: Chiasmus
notes.body: The words form an ABBA pattern: adjective, noun, noun, adjective. The neat pattern rounds off the picture of the empty camp.

notes.label: Epithet
notes.body: saevus reminds the reader of Achilles' terrible reputation. Even now he is gone, the Trojans remember him with fear.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: saevus and Achilles are split by tendebat, so the line ends on the hero's name. The reader is left with the memory of Troy's most feared enemy.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.body: hic is repeated again and again as the Trojans point out the sights. It sounds like eager sightseers saying "here was this, here was that".

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense makes the Trojans' amazement immediate, as if the reader stands beside them staring at the horse.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: formal epithet

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: innuptae and Minervae frame the deadly gift (donum exitiale), so the gift is enclosed by the goddess it is meant for. It hints that Minerva is bound up with Troy's ruin.

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense keeps the scene vivid as the crowd gazes at the horse.

notes.label: Variatio
notes.body: Two different verbs describe the Trojans' amazement. The variety stresses how awestruck they are by the horse.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: molem and equi are separated by mirantur. Putting molem first stresses the sheer size of the horse.

notes.label: Chiasmus
notes.trans: to be brought inside the walls and placed in the citadel
notes.body: The words form an ABBA pattern: verb, place, place, verb. The balanced phrase sounds like a confident proposal, which makes Thymoetes' advice seem persuasive.

notes.label: Delay
notes.body: fata is held near the end of the line, so the idea of fate lands with weight. Aeneas suggests that Troy's fall was already destined.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Thymoetes was a Trojan who had a grudge against Priam for putting his wife’s son to death to satisfy an oracle

notes.label: Comparative
notes.body: melior marks Capys and his supporters as wiser than the crowd. The reader is meant to side with them.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Lit. - [for those] of whom there was better sense of mind

notes.label: Vivid present
notes.body: The present tense makes the debate immediate, as if the reader can hear the competing voices.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: subiectis and flammis are separated by urere, so the flames seem to surround the act of burning. It makes the suggestion vivid and violent.

notes.label: Pregnancy vocabulary
notes.body: uterus again pictures the horse as pregnant with soldiers. The reader knows what the hollows really hide.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: Virgil also uses this in the blinding of the Cyclops.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.trans: to bore into the hollow hiding places and probe them
notes.body: Two matching infinitives with their objects (terebrare cavas, temptare latebras) set out the sensible plan. The balance shows how close the Trojans came to finding the Greeks.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: scinditur opens the line, so the division of the people is stressed. The Trojans' disagreement is what allows the horse to survive.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: incertum and volgus frame the line, with the opposing views in between. The word order mirrors a crowd pulled in two directions.

notes.label: Note
notes.body: not contemptuous. Virgil contrasts the rank and file with the names of the leaders.

notes.label: Mycenae
notes.body: The city of Agamemnon, leader of the Greek army; here it stands for Greece and home.

notes.label: Achilles
notes.body: The greatest Greek warrior at Troy, who killed Hector. He was already dead by the time of the wooden horse, but his camp is still pointed out.

notes.label: Minerva
notes.body: The Roman name for Pallas Athena, a virgin goddess (hence innuptae). The Greeks claimed the horse was an offering to her.

notes.label: Thymoetes and Capys
notes.body: Two Trojan elders. Thymoetes wants the horse brought into the city; Capys, the wiser, wants it destroyed. Capys later sailed with Aeneas to Italy.

questions: Why are the Trojans so happy to explore the Greek camp? How does Virgil make their relief clear?
Compare the advice of Thymoetes and Capys. Which does Aeneas, looking back, want us to agree with?
How does Virgil show that the Trojan people are divided at the end of this section?

context.body:
For ten years the Greeks had camped on the beach below Troy, with their ships drawn up on the shore. When the Trojans wake to find the camp empty and the fleet gone, they believe the war is over. In fact the Greek ships are hiding behind Tenedos, a few miles away.

The Trojans' first reaction is joy and curiosity: they wander round the camp pointing out where Achilles and his men had their tents. Then they come to the horse, and the city has to decide what to do with it. This debate is the first of several moments when Troy could still have been saved.
